name: Pyramid Principle (Minto)
use_case: My reports and e-mails to senior management are long and thorough, yet the readers have to dig through pages of background before they reach what I am asking them to decide, and they write back asking what I actually want from them; I need each document to open with the recommendation and then back it with a few grouped reasons in a deliberate order.
strengths: the reader learns the recommendation or request in the first lines and can stop reading once convinced
a short opening of situation, complication and question ties the answer to something the reader already accepts, without a long history
grouping the support into a few non-overlapping points shows the writer where an argument is missing or repeats itself
the same structure serves a two-line e-mail, a one-page memo, a long report and a slide deck
the top of the pyramid doubles as the executive summary and the subject line, so they no longer have to be written separately
a reviewer can check the logic by reading only the headings and first sentences
weaknesses: the writer must have reached a conclusion; it does not help while the thinking is still open
readers who expect the reasoning before the conclusion, as in some national and organisational cultures, can find an answer-first text abrupt or presumptuous
academic, legal and other genres with fixed conventions of their own do not fit the order
bad or unwelcome news stated in the first line can provoke rejection before the reasons are read
strictly non-overlapping groups are hard to find when the reasons are intertwined
the evidence is practitioner experience and consulting practice; controlled studies of the method itself are scarce
use_cases: How do I write a report or an e-mail to management so that the decision I need from them is clear in the first paragraph instead of buried under the background?

A school administrator prepares a briefing paper on a new timetable model for the school board, which reads it the evening before the meeting; last time the members spent the whole session asking what exactly they were being asked to approve.

A project lead's monthly status memo to the steering committee walks through every workstream in the order things happened, and the one item that needs the committee's approval, extra money for a supplier who is late, sits at the bottom and goes unnoticed.

An officer in a city administration needs the head of department to approve switching the old town's street lighting to LED; her draft memo reads like the history of the file, and she wants the request and its strongest reasons on the first half page.
audience: staff writing for management or boards
